This help sheet shows how to use built-in R procedures to carry out examples of matched pairs inference for means in Section 6.5. The primary R procedure for $t$ inference is `t.test()`. Note that the matched pairs design may typically be viewed simply as inference about a single mean, once differences in the matched pairs have been computed.

```{r,message=FALSE,echo=FALSE}
library(mosaic)
library(Lock5Data)
```

**Example 6.29 Matched Pairs Hypothesis Test**

```{r}
head(Wetsuits)
```

I recommend computing and saving the differences in the original data set and then plotting the data before proceeding.

The code below uses the `mutate()` command to compute and add a column of differences (Wetsuit-NoWet) to the original data set:

```{r}
Wetsuits <- mutate(Wetsuits, diff = Wetsuit - NoWetsuit)
```

Now plot a dotplot of the differences as shown in the text:

```{r}
gf_dotplot(~diff, data = Wetsuits)
```

Although it is difficult to see a bell-shape for samples this small, the differences look relatively symmetric and have no clear outliers, so we don’t detect any serious problems with normality and can proceed with the t-distribution.

Below is the R code for a one-sided hypothesis test.

```{r}
t.test(~diff, data = Wetsuits, alt = "greater")
```

The very large t-statistic and small p-value provide very convincing evidence that swimmers are faster on average when wearing wetsuits. Because this was a randomized experiment, we can conclude that wetsuits cause swimmers to swim faster.

**Example 6.30 Matched Pairs Confidence Interval**

Below is the R code for a 95% confidence interval. Note that 95% is the default value and need not be specified explicitly.

```{r}
t.test(~diff, data = Wetsuits, conf.level = .95)
```

We are 95% confident that for competitive swimmers and triathletes, wetsuits increase maximum swimming velocity by an average of between 0.064 and 0.091 meters per second.

Note: Occasionally it is useful to plot the paired values to verify the paired, correlated nature of the data. It is this correlation that provides the gain in sensitivity of paired t analysis compared to the independent two samples t method.

```{r}
cor(Wetsuit ~ NoWetsuit, data = Wetsuits)
```

A plot of the paired data verifies the high correlation meaning that the fastest swimmers are fastest regardless of whether they are wearing a wetsuit or not.

```{r}
gf_point(Wetsuit ~ NoWetsuit, data = Wetsuits)
```
